newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu return gives Zaireans excuse to celebrate.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu return gives Zaireans excuse to celebrate.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, looking older and frailer after cancer surgery, stepped back into the maelstrom of Zairean politics on Tuesday and provided his chaotic nation with a rare excuse for celebration.
The veteran leader, wearing his trade-mark leopard-skin hat, held himself erect as the national anthem sounded round the international airport outside the capital Kinshasa.
Well over a hundred thousand supporters waved banners and danced and cheered to the sound of brass bands, drums and music both at the airport and along the route to and through the capital.

But the nation seemed to be holding its breath to see whether he could conjure up solutions to end a Tutsi-led revolt that has routed Zaire's demoralised army in the east and presented him with one of his toughest challenges in three decades in power.
"It's a great day. It's like the return of a father," one Mobutu supporter told Reuters.
"Thing's have not been going well. It's great to see him back," a banner-wielding teenaged commented.
The crowds, a handful wearing imitation leopard-skin hats, many more dressed in shirts or dresses bearing Mobutu's image, surged forward as the plane taxied to a halt.
Mobutu, 66, smiled broadly as he walked down the steps from the aircraft with his wife, Bobi Ladawa, as cheering, drumming, music and chanting sounded around the airport.
He walked unaided and easily, carrying, as always, a carved walking stick.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo waited at the aircraft steps. No opposition personalities were in evidence.
Two young girls in white dresses handed him bouquets.
Mobutu shook hands all round and joined in singing the national anthem. He raised his arms in acknowledgement, as the crowd burst into cheering.
Mobutu and his wife later left by car for his official residence in the capital with the fiercely loyal presidential guard protecting their convoy.
Cheering crowds and curious onlookers lined the route and thronged the streets of the teeming populous districts of the capital as Mobutu drove by.
Banners at the airport called for action to end the revolt in the east, but there is also an undercurrent of dissatisfaction as ordinary people find it harder to make ends meet.
Since foreign and domestic pressure forced him to start embracing democracy change in 1990, Mobutu has preferred to remain in his jungle palace of Gbadolite in the northern Equateur Region.

All his recent appearances in the capital have been linked to crises -- in 1995 it was the Ebola virus, in January 1996 an air disaster in which a Russian plane ploughed into a market killing more than 300 people.
